summary: YANG is a data modeling language for configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications used by network management protocols. This proposed standard describes the syntax and semantics of version 1.1, a maintenance release that fixes ambiguities and defects in the original.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is a language for describing the settings, meters, operations and alerts of a network device, so that management software and the device agree on what the data means. Version 1.1 repairs confusing spots in the first version and adds a few missing pieces. It does not replace the first version.

subtitle: The language network engineers use to describe, as a typed tree, every setting, meter, operation and alert a managed device exposes.

tldr.problem: Network management protocols such as NETCONF need a precise, machine-readable way to describe configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications, so that clients and servers agree on what the data means.
tldr.mechanism: YANG organizes data as a tree of modules containing leaf, leaf-list, container and list nodes with typed values and constraints. Groupings, augments, features and deviations let models be reused, extended and honestly adapted to what a server supports. Version 1.1 also defines how this data is encoded in XML and manipulated with NETCONF.
tldr.outcome: YANG 1.1 is a maintenance release of the original YANG that fixes ambiguities and defects, with a small number of backward incompatibilities. It does not obsolete RFC 6020, and it has since been updated by RFC 8342 and RFC 8526.

today: RFC 7950 is a Proposed Standard that does not obsolete RFC 6020, and it has been updated by RFC 8342 and RFC 8526.

sections.title: What YANG Is For
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language. It was originally designed to model the configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF), plus NETCONF Remote Procedure Calls and notifications. Since the publication of YANG version 1 in RFC 6020, YANG has also been used or proposed for other protocols, such as RESTCONF and the Constrained Application Protocol Management Interface, and encodings other than XML have been proposed, such as JSON in RFC 7951.

This document describes the syntax and semantics of version 1.1 of the language. It also says how data defined in a YANG module is encoded in XML and how NETCONF operations manipulate it. Other protocols and encodings are out of scope. The RFC states that it does not obsolete RFC 6020.

Version 1.1 is a maintenance release, addressing ambiguities and defects in the original specification. A small number of changes are not backward compatible: the escape rules inside double-quoted strings changed, unquoted strings cannot contain quote characters, when and if-feature are illegal on list keys, the legal characters in a module are now defined, and noncharacters are illegal in the string type.

New in 1.1 are, among others, the action statement, notifications tied to data nodes, the anydata statement, boolean expressions in if-feature, leaf-lists with default values, enumerations and bits that can be subtyped, identities derived from multiple base identities, and a set of new XPath functions.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is a single, strict way to write the manual for a network device, so a computer can read it. Version 1.1 fixes places where the first version was confusing and adds a few pieces that were missing.

sections.title: The Data Tree and Its Node Kinds
sections.content:
YANG models data as a tree in which each node has a name and either a value or a set of child nodes. Four node kinds do most of the work.

  • A leaf holds exactly one value of a particular type and has no child nodes, for example a host name.
  • A leaf-list defines a sequence of values of one type, such as a list of domain names to search.
  • A container groups related nodes in a subtree. It has child nodes but no value of its own.
  • A list defines a sequence of entries, each like a container. Entries are uniquely identified by the values of the list's key leafs.

Containers come in two styles. A non-presence container exists only to organize the hierarchy, so an empty one means the same as an absent one. A presence container, marked with the presence statement, means something by existing; in the RFC's example, an ssh container whose presence enables SSH.

A choice contains case branches whose nodes cannot appear together. Choice and case nodes exist only in the schema tree, not in the data tree. When a node from one case is created, all nodes from every other case are implicitly deleted by the server.

YANG also separates settings from measurements with the config statement. A node tagged config false marks its whole subhierarchy as state data; config true marks configuration data. If config is omitted, a node inherits its parent's value, and the top-level default is true. Nothing under a config false node can be config true. In the RFC's interface example, a speed leaf is configuration while an observed-speed leaf is state.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings on a device form a tree, like folders inside folders. A leaf is one named value, a container is a folder, and a list is a stack of identical forms distinguished by a name field. A choice is a menu: only one of its branches may be used at a time.

sections.title: Modules, Submodules and Namespaces
sections.content:
The module is the base unit of definition. A module defines a single data model, or augments an existing one. Its header carries yang-version, namespace and prefix, followed by imports, includes, meta-information such as organization and contact, a revision history, and then the definitions. Within a server, all module names MUST be unique, and the RFC recommends names unlikely to collide, for example by using an organization name as a prefix.

A submodule is a partial module. A module may include any number of submodules, but each submodule belongs to only one module, and the outside world still sees a single module. In version 1.1 a submodule can reference definitions in all submodules of its module without using include.

The import statement makes another module's definitions available under a local prefix, written as prefix:name. An import may pin a specific revision-date, which protects the importing module when the imported one evolves: future revisions do not affect it until the author republishes with the new revision. If no revision is given, it is undefined which revision is used, and there MUST NOT be circular chains of imports.

Each module is bound to a distinct XML namespace, a globally unique URI. Namespaces for modules published in RFC streams MUST be assigned by IANA; private namespaces are chosen by the owning organization. YANG itself defines the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:1 for NETCONF edit-config operations, error-info content and the action element. Files are typically named after the module, with the extension .yang for YANG syntax or .yin for YIN syntax, optionally with the revision date after an at-sign.

Names of groupings, types and identities are resolved where they are defined, not where they are used, like static scoping in a programming language. Typedefs and groupings can be nested under statements, which keeps them private to a module or submodule, since only top-level definitions can be used from outside.
sections.plainLanguage: A module is like a recipe book with its own name and cover. It can borrow a recipe from another book, but must say which book and which edition, so nothing changes under it by surprise. Each module also owns a unique web address that labels its data on the wire.

sections.title: Built-In Types, Derived Types and Constraints
sections.content:
Every leaf has a type. YANG has a set of built-in types, from the familiar integers (int8 through int64, uint8 through uint64), string, boolean and binary, to management-specific ones: bits (a set of flags), enumeration, decimal64, empty, union, leafref, identityref and instance-identifier.

New types are derived with typedef from a built-in type or another derived type, and can restrict the base with a range, length or pattern. The RFC's example is a percent type that is a uint8 restricted to the range 0 .. 100. A decimal64 must give a fraction-digits argument between 1 and 18, inclusive. A leafref points at another leaf through a path, and by default the referenced instance must exist. An identityref names an identity; valid values are those derived from its base identities.

Values are stored in canonical form, and a server sending XML must use the canonical form. A default value applies when a leaf is absent, subject to its ancestors and any when or if-feature condition.

YANG models can state constraints that valid data must obey. Leaf values must match their type restrictions, all list keys must be present, at most one case of a choice may have nodes, and a must statement holds an XPath expression that MUST evaluate to true. Other constraints are unique for lists, min-elements and max-elements, mandatory, and referential integrity through leafref paths. The running configuration datastore MUST always be valid. For NETCONF, constraints are enforced while parsing payloads, while processing edit-config, and at validation time; for the candidate datastore, enforcement waits for a commit or validate operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each value on the form has a declared kind, such as a whole number in a range or one of a fixed set of words. Derived types narrow a base type, for example a whole number from 0 to 100. The model can also state rules that valid data must obey, and the device must keep its configuration inside those rules at all times.

sections.title: Reuse and Extension
sections.content:
A grouping is a reusable set of schema nodes. It defines nothing by itself; a uses statement instantiates it, and refine can tailor the instance, for example by replacing a description, adding a default, or changing mandatory or min-elements. The RFC shows one target grouping, an address and a port, used for both the source and the destination of a connection.

The augment statement adds nodes to a schema tree defined elsewhere, including in another module, which the RFC says is useful for vendors adding vendor-specific parameters to standard data models in an interoperable way. When a server implements a module containing an augment, the augmented module's implementation contains the added nodes. The added XML elements are qualified by the augmenting module's namespace. If an augment adds mandatory configuration nodes to another module's node, it MUST be made conditional with when, so that clients that do not know the augmenting module do not break.

An identity is a globally unique, abstract, untyped name that may be derived from one or more base identities. Version 1.1 explicitly allows multiple bases. Together with the identityref type this gives an extensible set of named values.

Finally, the extension statement lets standards bodies, vendors and individuals define new statements that carry non-YANG semantics. When an extension is used, its keyword MUST be qualified with the prefix of the module that defines it, and the syntax makes extensions stand out from standard statements. A parser that does not support an extension MAY ignore it entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: A grouping is a cookie cutter you can press out again and again, adjusting the dough slightly each time. An augment adds extra settings to someone else's model without changing the original. An identity is a name that can have sub-names, so new kinds of values can be added later without touching old code.

sections.title: Operations and Notifications
sections.content:
YANG can describe things a device does, not just what it stores. An rpc defines a top-level operation with an optional input and output, whose parameters are modeled with ordinary data definition statements. The RFC's example is activate-software-image, with an image-name input and a status output, carried in a NETCONF rpc and rpc-reply.

Version 1.1 adds the action statement, an operation tied to a specific container or list data node. The RFC states the difference plainly: an action is tied to a node in the datastore, whereas an rpc is not, so invoking an action names the node along with the action and its input. An action cannot be defined inside an rpc, another action or a notification, and cannot sit under a list that has no key. In XML, actions travel inside an action element in the YANG namespace.

A notification defines an event message, with its content modeled by data definition statements. In 1.1 a notification can be defined at the top level of a module or attached to a container or list node. The RFC's example is a link-failure notification carrying an interface name, which is a leafref to /interface/name, together with the interface's administrative and operational status.

Because input and notification trees are not part of any datastore, config statements inside them are ignored. Mandatory leafs must be present, and defaults apply as they do for leafs elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides stored settings and readings, a device can offer buttons and alarms. An rpc is a button on the control panel. An action is a button that belongs to one particular interface or list entry. A notification is an alarm message the device sends when something happens.

sections.title: Syntax, XPath and YIN
sections.content:
YANG syntax is C-like, chosen for readability. Every statement is a keyword, zero or one argument, and either a semicolon or a block in braces. Comments are C++ style. Modules are stored in files using the UTF-8 character encoding, and the legal characters in a module exclude the C0 control characters other than tab, carriage return and line feed, the surrogate blocks and the noncharacters.

Strings can be unquoted, single-quoted, in which every character is preserved, or double-quoted, in which a backslash escapes only a newline, a tab, a double quote or a backslash. Quoted strings can be joined with +. Identifiers start with an ASCII letter or underscore and are case sensitive, and implementations MUST support identifiers up to 64 characters in length.

Many references and dependencies use XML Path Language (XPath) 1.0 as notation: the must, when and path statements, and in 1.1 the if-feature argument. An implementation does not have to contain an XPath interpreter, but it MUST enforce the requirements the model encodes. The data tree has no document order, so expressions SHOULD NOT depend on one. XPath numbers are double-precision floating point, so some 64-bit values cannot be represented exactly and equality comparisons on them can give unexpected results. Section 10 adds the functions current(), re-match(), deref(), derived-from(), derived-from-or-self(), enum-value() and bit-is-set().

YIN is an XML form of the same information, with one YIN element per YANG keyword, so that XML tools such as XSLT validators can work on models. The mapping is semantically lossless and can be round-tripped, though comments and whitespace are not preserved. YIN elements live in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:yin:1. The full YANG grammar is given in ABNF in Section 14.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is written like tidy recipe cards: a keyword, an optional name, then either a semicolon or a braced block. It borrows XPath, the query language of XML, to state rules that refer to other parts of the tree. YIN is the same model rewritten as XML so ordinary XML tools can process it.

sections.title: Features, Deviations and Errors
sections.content:
Conformance is a measure of how accurately a server follows a data model. YANG modelers have three mechanisms. The basic behavior of the model is a contract between a YANG-based client and server about the syntax and semantics of the data. A feature marks parts of the model as optional, and if-feature ties definitions to a feature; in 1.1 the if-feature argument is a boolean expression over feature names. If a server does not support a feature, those parts of the module are not valid on that server, and applications should behave accordingly.

A deviation lets a server declare how it fails to implement part of a module, using deviate with not-supported, add, replace or delete. The RFC's example is a BGP model that allows any number of peers while a particular server supports only 16, so an application can know the limit before it fails. The RFC says deviations are strongly discouraged, are a last resort, and must never be part of a published standard.

A NETCONF server MUST announce the modules it implements through the ietf-yang-library module, listing them in the /modules-state/module list, and MUST advertise a yang-library capability in its hello message with revision and module-set-id parameters. A server MUST NOT implement more than one revision of a module.

Section 15 defines NETCONF error responses for YANG-related violations. A broken unique constraint returns operation-failed with the error-app-tag data-not-unique; a broken must returns must-violation; a leafref or instance-identifier that points at a missing instance returns data-missing with instance-required; and an empty mandatory choice returns missing-choice. A specific error-app-tag substatement on the YANG statement overrides the default.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is only useful if the machine follows it. YANG lets a model mark optional parts as features, and lets a server admit the exact places where it does not follow the model, so control software can plan around the limits instead of failing late.

sections.title: Updating Modules and Living with Version 1
sections.content:
Published modules have to evolve without breaking clients written against earlier versions. For any published change, a new revision statement MUST be added in front of the existing ones. The module name and the namespace MUST NOT be changed, and obsolete definitions MUST NOT be removed, since other modules may still reference them.

The allowed revisions only widen or add: new enums or bits without changing existing values, an expanded range, length or pattern, a new default on a leaf that has none, a relaxed must, when or mandatory, relaxed min-elements or max-elements, a status moved from current to deprecated to obsolete, and new typedefs, groupings, features, identities, rpcs, notifications and extensions. New data definition nodes may be added if they are not mandatory, or if they depend on a new feature. Data definition substatements MUST NOT be reordered. Any other change that alters the meaning of a definition MUST be made as a new definition with a new identifier.

Version 1 and version 1.1 modules can coexist, within limits. A 1.1 module MUST NOT include a version 1 submodule, and the reverse is also forbidden. A version 1 module MUST NOT import a 1.1 module by revision, while a 1.1 module MAY import a version 1 module by revision. The RFC explains that this avoids a cascade in which updating one module to 1.1 would force every module that imports it to be updated too. A module with no yang-version statement, or with the value 1, is a version 1 module as defined in RFC 6020; version 1.1 modules MUST say 1.1.

One change to NETCONF advertising is also worth knowing: a server advertises support for YANG 1.1 modules through ietf-yang-library rather than listing them as capabilities in the hello message.
sections.plainLanguage: Old rulebooks cannot be changed in ways that make old legal moves illegal. So YANG only allows changes that widen or add; anything that changes meaning needs a brand-new name. A version 1.1 module can still use older version 1 modules, but not the other way round.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the language itself has no security impact on the Internet. The same considerations apply as for the base NETCONF protocol in RFC 6241. Data modeled in YANG might contain sensitive information, and RPCs or notifications defined in YANG might transfer it. Security issues are related to the usage of the data and are to be handled in the documents describing the data models and the interfaces used to manipulate the data, such as the NETCONF documents.

Such data depends on the security of the transmission infrastructure used to send it, the security of the applications that store or release it, and adequate authentication and access control mechanisms to restrict its use. The RFC also warns tool authors that YANG parsers need to be robust with respect to malformed documents: reading malformed documents from unknown or untrusted sources could result in an attacker gaining the privileges of the user running the parser, and in an extreme situation the entire machine could be compromised.

The only IANA action is the registration of one NETCONF capability identifier, :yang-library, with the URN urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:yang-library:1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook itself is not dangerous, but the data it describes can hold secrets, so the network, the applications and access control must all be trustworthy. Any program that reads YANG files must also be careful with broken files from strangers.

items.title: Basic behavior
items.text: The model is a contract between client and server about the syntax and semantics of the data.

items.title: Features
items.text: The feature and if-feature statements mark parts of the model that a server may or may not support.

items.title: Deviations
items.text: The deviation statement declares where a server fails to follow the model. A last resort.
